title: Achieving Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning via Layer-Adaptive Sparsified Model Aggregation

C-a.quote: LASA consists of three key components to achieve Byzantine resilience, we conduct an ablation study to investigate how each component functions. We denote pre-aggregation sparsification, magnitude-based adaptive filtering, and direction-based adaptive filtering as Spar, Ma, and Di, respectively.
C-a.locator: §5.3 (ablation study); the three stages are applied in that order within one round, and the stated purpose of the FIRST stage is defense, not compression -- "reducing the impact of malicious parameters and minimizing the interference from less important parameters for the subsequent filtering process. Based on sparsified updates, a layer-wise adaptive filter then adaptively selects benign layers using both magnitude a[nd direction]" (§4). The two filters' purposes are stated at §4, "both magnitude and direction of each model update are captured at the layer level to effectively identify and filter out malicious clients"

C-b.quote: direction-based adaptive filtering is powerful in defending against the stealthy Min-Max and Lie attacks, but it is vulnerable to the simple Noise attack that generates malicious updates with large magnitudes.
C-b.locator: §5.3; the converse half is in the adjacent sentence, "magnitude-based adaptive filtering is effective in defending against Noise attack but is less effective against MinMax and Lie attacks", which is complementary threat coverage stated as a matched pair. The upstream stage's pairing reason is separate and is a serve-the-downstream reason: "minimizing the interference from less important parameters for the subsequent filtering process" (§4). The deficiency of the alternatives is given at §2, "model-wise methods [7, 16, 42, 45, 58] overlook the diverse distribution of direction and magnitude across layers, limiting their robustness"

C-c.quote: accuracy under all attacks, outperforming other defense methods. For example, under ByzMean attack, LASA, GeoMed, and SignGuard stand out as the most effective defense methods on FMNIST, and LASA achieves the highest accuracy
C-c.locator: §5.2; the metric is the assembled system's own robust accuracy under Noise, Sign-Flipping, ByzMean, Min-Max and Lie attacks across IID and non-IID datasets

C-d.quote: Notably, when integrated with preaggregation sparsification, the performance of directionbased adaptive filtering improves: the accuracy of Spar+Di is higher than that of Di. This demonstrates the effectiveness of sparsification in improving the filtering accuracy.
C-d.locator: §5.3, Table 3 ("Comparison of Performance with Different Components"), whose arms are Spar / Ma / Di / Spar+Ma / Spar+Di / Ma+Di / LASA (Ours). The Di vs Spar+Di pair holds the downstream filter fixed and toggles only the upstream sparsification; the Ma+Di vs LASA pair does the same with both filters downstream. coder_note:
THIS IS THE STRICTEST C-d IN THE FRAME AND THE PAPER READS THE CONTRAST IN THE RUBRIC'S OWN DIRECTION, UNPROMPTED. Table 3's arms include Di alone and Spar+Di, and §5.3 states the comparison between exactly those two arms, in words: integrating the upstream sparsification IMPROVES the downstream direction-based filter, therefore sparsification improves filtering accuracy. The downstream mechanism is held fixed, the upstream stage is the only thing varied, and the conclusion drawn is about the downstream mechanism's behavior under a changed input. That is Prop. prop:identification_full's contrast, run by a third party, and it is a stronger instance than FLAME's or SPFL's because it is a toggle of an upstream stage rather than a substitution inside one. Rule 4's benefit of the doubt is not needed anywhere in this row.

AND THE PAPER THEN DEMONSTRATES OUR THESIS AGAINST ITSELF, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ROW. The composed-system comparison does NOT justify the upstream stage: LASA (Spar+Ma+Di) is only "comparable performance to Ma+Di", i.e. adding Spar to the full downstream buys approximately nothing on the outcome metric, and the paper says so. Having run the identifying contrast, it can still fall back on the C-d evidence and the theory of §4.1 to argue the component is necessary -- "we emphasize in Section 4.1 the theoretical significance of Spar in enhancing robustness, thereby underscoring its necessity." A paper that had only the composed number would have had to drop the stage or assert its value. This is a live external instance of a composed evaluation FAILING to identify a constituent's contribution, and of the within-defense contrast rescuing the conclusion. A4 and A5 should use it, and it is worth more to the argument than a primary = YES row, because it shows the identification problem is real and consequential in practice rather than merely possible.

AMENDMENT 3 RAISES A CODE HERE FOR THE SECOND TIME. The first stage is called SPARSIFICATION and, read by the operation's name, it is a compression device and C-a would code NO on one mechanism -- and then the frame would lose its strictest C-d row. §4's stated purpose is defense: reduce the impact of malicious parameters and reduce interference for the subsequent filter. Amendment 3 was disclosed as being able only to LOWER the primary and DESIGN rates; Fedward (2307.00356) and now LASA are two rows where it raises them, and in this row it raises the C-d rate too. A5 must state the amendment's raising direction and name both papers.

WHY THIS ROW IS DESIGN = YES BUT PRIMARY = NO, AND WHY THAT IS THE POINT. C-a, C-b, C-c and C-e are all YES: three stated defense stages, an explicit complementary-threat pairing reason with both halves quoted, robust accuracy of the assembled system, and an attributional claim naming a constituent's contribution. The single reason it is not outcome-gated is C-d, and C-d is present because this paper did the work. That is the audit's cleanest contrast with Fedward and BRFL, which have the identical design and no internal contrast at all.
